displayQuote: It takes a lot of time to be a genius, you have to sit around so much doing nothing

meta.title: Who really said "It takes a lot of time to be a genius, you have to sit around so much doing nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Gertrude Stein really wrote it, in Everybody's Autobiography (1937). The line is usually quoted truncated; her sentence ends "really doing nothing."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It takes a lot of time to be a genius, you have to sit around so much doing nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Gertrude Stein — from Everybody's Autobiography (1937), Ch. 2. Most versions drop her closing words, "really doing nothing."

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Stein wrote this in Everybody’s Autobiography (Random House, 1937), where it appears in Chapter 2. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ ties it to that work. The popular form is slightly clipped — her full sentence closes “…so much doing nothing, really doing nothing.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: It takes a lot of time to be a genius, you have to sit around so much doing nothing, really doing nothing.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section under Everybody’s Autobiography (1937), Ch. 2 — not among misattributed or disputed lines.
First-edition catalog records confirm Everybody’s Autobiography was published by Random House in 1937 ↗, Stein’s sequel to The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas.
Quote databases such as QuotePark ↗ reproduce the same wording and cite the same 1937 work and chapter.
source.excerptNote: The widely shared version stops at “doing nothing”; Stein’s own sentence repeats the phrase for emphasis — “really doing nothing.”

author.name: Gertrude Stein
author.heading: About the author
author.metaLine: 1874–1946 · American modernist writer, poet & art collector
author.bio: Gertrude Stein was an American expatriate writer whose Paris salon at 27 rue de Fleurus was a hub of early-20th-century modernism, mentoring figures from Picasso to Hemingway. Known for her playful, repetitive prose, she wrote The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas (1933) and its sequel Everybody’s Autobiography (1937). Her wry aphorisms — often about genius, which she cheerfully claimed for herself — are among the most quoted lines of the era.

misattribution.heading: Set the record straight
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Stein — the problem is how it travels, not whether she said it.

items.why: The line is almost always cut short at “so much doing nothing.” Stein’s sentence in Everybody’s Autobiography repeats the idea — “really doing nothing” — which is part of her characteristic style. See Wikiquote ↗.
The quip circulates with no book named, which is why it gets lumped in with the many fabricated “Stein” lines. It is real — and it has an address: Everybody’s Autobiography (1937), Ch. 2.

misattribution.truthLine: Authentic Gertrude Stein, from Everybody’s Autobiography (1937) ↗ — just usually quoted a few words short.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Stein was only half-joking. She genuinely believed genius required unstructured, apparently idle time — the mental wandering out of which her experimental writing came. Placed in Everybody’s Autobiography, the remark is of a piece with her lifelong, self-assured insistence that she was a genius, delivered with a deadpan wit that made the boast go down easily.

The line endures because it flatters the daydreamer in everyone: it reframes doing nothing as creative labor. That is also why it’s so easy to strip from its source and paste onto a productivity meme — the sentiment survives even when the citation falls away.
context.pull: It takes a lot of time to be a genius… really doing nothing.
